title: Strong on three dimensions, absent on the fourth
context: SYNTHETIC SCENARIO (no real employee data). Ravi is up for L6/staff. This company's L6 rubric has four core, non-negotiable dimensions: (1) technical depth, (2) cross-org influence, (3) driving technical strategy, and (4) sustained delivery of ambiguous, high-impact work. Ravi is exceptional — well above the L6 bar — on technical depth, cross-org influence, and sustained delivery. On the fourth, driving technical strategy, there is no evidence: he executes strategy others set and has not originated org-level technical direction. A calibration reviewer proposes: 'He's outstanding on three of four and only average-to-absent on one, so on balance he clears L6 — the strengths more than compensate.' The rubric describes the four dimensions as requirements a staff engineer must all meet, not a weighted scorecard to average.
question: Does Ravi meet the L6 bar, and how should the four dimensions be applied?
gold_notes: When a rubric defines core dimensions as requirements (must-haves), leveling is gated by the weakest core dimension, not the average — a missing must-have caps the level.
Ravi has no evidence on 'driving technical strategy', a stated core L6 requirement, so exceptional performance elsewhere does not backfill that gap.
Treating the rubric as a weighted average lets strengths mask an unmet requirement — that is a leveling error, not generosity.
Correct call: not yet L6; place at L5 (likely top of band given his strengths) with a development path targeting the specific missing dimension (originating org-level technical strategy).
Distinguish 'compensating strengths' (valid for a scorecard) from 'unmet requirement' (a gate) — core rubric dimensions are gates.
trap: Averaging across the four dimensions — 'outstanding on three, weak on one, so on balance L6' — when the rubric defines them as must-have requirements, so an unmet core dimension should cap the level rather than being outweighed by strengths.
